messages.subject: Can one skip steps in model comparison?
messages.subject_clean: Can one skip steps in model comparison?
messages.body_plain:
Hello List,

 

For the analysis of a fully controlled experiment (i.e., same amount of data
for all combinations of fixed effects),

I had recently come across an example where a base model (intercept only
plus maximal random effect structure),
was compared with the full two-factorial model (two main effects plus
interaction, same random effect structure).

 

If that comparison is not significant, can one conclude that none of the
factors matter?

 

All text books on regression make step-wise comparisons, so I would think
no, but I have never seen that written anywhere.

I would intuitively say that one significant predictor and two insignificant
one can make the overall comparison insignificant.

But then the Bayesian guys have taught me to never trust my intuition.

 

Kind regards,

Holger

messages.body_plain:
Hi Holger,

What you are referring to is a multiparameter test of the fixed effects 
defining the main effects and interactions of interest, which is 
tantamount to a good old-fashioned "omnibus" ANOVA.  e.g., for a 2x2 
design it would be testing B1 = B2 = B3 = 0.

I'm not really sure why anyone would ever do such a test, because (as 
your intuition suggests) you could have a nonsignificant omnibus test 
with some individual factors significant, if tested individually, and 
others nonsignificant.  In effect, the omnibus test diffuses your power 
across all factors in the design.  It's typically more sensible to go in 
and test your theoretically-relevant hypothesis individually, using as 
much power as possible.  Perhaps an omnibus test could be used in an 
exploratory situation, where you want to know if anything matters, and 
are worried about error control.

-D

messages.body_plain:
Holger,

In addition to  what Dale said, a few details:

> On Feb 16, 2016, at 3:11 AM, Holger Mitterer <holger.mitterer-Mj5aoWcxWbpeoWH0uzbU5w at public.gmane.org> wrote:

> For the analysis of a fully controlled experiment (i.e., same amount of data for all combinations of fixed effects),

I would call that a “balanced" design.

> I had recently come across an example where a base model (intercept only plus maximal random effect structure),
> was compared with the full two-factorial model (two main effects plus interaction, same random effect structure).
>  
> If that comparison is not significant, can one conclude that none of the factors matter?

Non-significance does not indicate that an effect does not exist.  Hence, in principle you cannot conclude that certain factors do not matter.  Also, it seems that this model comparison would just evaluate the relative contribution of all interactions as a whole to the model.  You can still not conclude that they do not matter.  You can only conclude that you do not have evidence to say that all of the interactions, in combination, do not make a significant contribution to the model.  (If you know you have sufficient power and/or p>0.8, you could begin to think about drawing the “does not matter” conclusion.)

>  All text books on regression make step-wise comparisons, so I would think no, but I have never seen that written anywhere.
> I would intuitively say that one significant predictor and two insignificant one can make the overall comparison insignificant.

Ignoring noise, a single significant predictor would make the model comparison significant, even if there are many non-significant ones in the mix.  In practice, however, the power is reduced as Dale pointed out.

Keep in mind that there are issues with step-wise regression that have to do with the order of factors (determined by no good principle) and collinearity.

--
Dr. David Reitter
Assistant Professor of Information Sciences and Technology
Co-Director, Applied Cognitive Science Lab
The Pennsylvania State University
http://www.david-reitter.com

logistic models to linguistic data. I am having difficulty finding
information on how to obtain a specific contrast in a 3-way interaction of

I've attached the data. Meanwhile I found this website which seems to offer
a solution to both questions:

http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/r/faq/testing_contrasts.htm

Applied to my case:

#all pairwise comparisons
#creating a new BIG variable

mydata$newvariable <- with(data, interaction(Syntax, Animacy, Prof.group.2,
sep = "x"))

head(mydata$newvariable)


#data$newvariable is then inserted into a model with a single predictor:

m2 <- bglmer(Correct ~ newvariable+(1|Part.name) +(1|Item), data =
mydata, Control:
glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"), family = binomial)

l2 <- glht(m2, linfct = mcp(tall = "Tukey"))

summary(l2)

What I'm still not convinced about is why the model shouldn't include the
main effects (at least that's what the source suggests). If I add the main
effects, the following error is returned:

fixed-effect model matrix is rank deficient so dropping 4 columns /
coefficients

As it stands it looks like another way of rehashing the original final
model with all interactions defined and called.

If I try this solution without the main effects it works fine and all
possible pairwise interactions are shown, which is very useful but I'm not
entirely sure is foolproof.

Another issue I have is with the test type fed to mcp. Can I use Turkey to
evaluate log odds coefficients?

F.

Florian, I'm keeping R-ling in the thread as other people might benefit
from our exchange.
Thanks for your suggestions. Just to be clear my question was not why I
shouldn't run:

Correct ~ newvariable+Syntax+Animacy+(1|Part.name) +(1|Item)?

There should also be a Prof.group.2 (3-level) categorical predictor in
there. I'm seeking multiple post-hoc comparisons for a 2x2x3 matrix leading
to 66 comparisons. Next, there doesn't seem to be much leverage in terms of
the tests to be fed to mcp. I could only find a Dunnett option for
non-parametric tests but results do not change anyway. Also, although the
vcov function would be ideal it is not compatible with glmer. There is a
covar.equal = T/F and covar_average = T/F but I'm not sure that applies in
this case. The Shaffer and Westfall tests you suggested do not work with
linfct.

The multcomp is a powerful package well-suited to solve the issues raised,
in my opinion.
